Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can I earn money with a game development company? If the games you make aren't successful, you just lose a lot of money.
Answer: Use the Mel Brooks approach from The Producers. Convince a lot of investors up front that you’re going to make an amazing game, then spend less than they invested. Voila - Profit! The game, and your investors, lose money, but some of it has been transferred to you. Of course, making a profit honorably and honestly is much harder. Make an excellent game that fills a niche in the market, and promote it heavily; then you might have a chance of making money. I might recommend books by Seth Godin on how to have a massive marketing impact with a small dollar investment. Of course, every dollar you don’t spend has to be “paid for” in work effort by yourself and your team; nothing is free. I’m personally rather lazy and poor at this. Others are more successful, but from what I can see, that isn’t many of them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does your solo games have to be successful in order to join the game industry? I have 5 published (but not promoted) mobile games and keep getting rejected when I apply as a unity developer to a game company outside my country. What more should do?
Answer: Getting a job in game development is largely up to luck and connections. If you know someone who works for a particular company, and they refer you, that will greatly help your chances. If not, you just need to keep trying. Think of every job application as accompanied by a dice roll. If the dice go your way, you’ll get an interview, and possibly eventually an offer. Other factors such as connections and your previous experience give you modifiers to your rolls, but you still need luck. “Outside my country” is also an issue. For a U.S. company to hire someone from another country, they need to go through hoops to get you a rare work visa. They will also expect to need to pay you relocation expenses, which makes it more affordable to hire someone local. But the job opportunities are out there. All you can do is keep trying, build some connections through conferences and online game development boards. With enough persistence, your number will eventually come up.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do software engineers consider as a failure when they are asked in an interview if they have failed at something?
Answer: A lot of people answer that question with a self-serving answer that doesn’t really show a failure at all. But everyone fails. Those who become successful learn from their failures and strive to do better the next time. I had a task that failed because I tried to push it through to QA too quickly; I should have tested it more first, even if it meant delaying the product schedule. I’ve had several projects cancelled, or stopped them when they were incomplete. I could easily talk about those, to what degree I was responsible, and how I would try to prevent cancellation of a future project. I haven’t applied to a new job for a while, but if I did, I would consider this a test of the interviewer as much as of me. If he or she reacts poorly to an honest example of a failure, then I probably don’t want to work there. Good managers know that failure is an inevitable part of the process, and learning from failure is essential to doing a good job.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I’m interested in getting into game development, and I’m wondering what steps one should take to get into the industry? I think I should focus on programming initially, and I could look into/try other aspects of game dev later in my career if I want.
Answer: That depends totally on your skills and interests. If you enjoy wrangling computer code to teach a dumb machine how to look intelligent, then programming is for you. You could become a software engineer in a company’s tools group, a server software developer focusing on the world content, or a client developer focusing on presentation. If you love drawing and painting, you can get into creating game art and animation. There are hundreds of specialties in game development, with thousands of sub-specialties. Find your affinity, then focus on that.
